title: How to Calculate Sinking Funds for Annual Expenses: 6 Examples
meta_description: Learn how to calculate sinking funds for annual expenses with one formula, 6 worked examples, catch-up tips and a copy-ready spreadsheet tracker.
quick_answer: A sinking fund is money you save in regular amounts for a known future bill. To calculate one for an annual expense, use (target amount − amount already saved) ÷ monthly contributions left before the due date. A $1,200 insurance bill due in 12 months needs $100 a month. Round up, automate the transfer, and after paying the bill, switch to the annual cost ÷ 12.
key_takeaways: Use one formula for every fund: (target − already saved) ÷ contributions left before the due date, then round up.
Count the transfers you'll actually make before the bill is due, not calendar months. If you save from each paycheck, count paydays instead.
For costs with no fixed date, like car, home or pet repairs, save your yearly estimate ÷ 12 into a rolling fund with a cap.
Starting late means a higher payment for a while. Once the bill is paid, drop back to annual cost ÷ 12.
Add up every fund's monthly amount before you commit. If the total doesn't fit, fund essential bills first and give flexible goals more time.
Keep sinking funds in cash and separate from your emergency fund. Check deposit protection, fees and the tax rules where you live.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for anyone on a monthly budget who keeps getting caught out by once-a-year bills like insurance, renewals, holidays, gifts or home repairs, and wants to turn them into steady, predictable monthly amounts.
intro: Annual bills shouldn't come as a surprise. Car insurance, subscription renewals and the holidays arrive on roughly the same date every year, yet they still wreck plenty of monthly budgets. A sinking fund fixes that by splitting each big cost into small monthly amounts. This guide gives you the formula and works through six common examples with round numbers. It also covers the three situations that trip people up most: money you've already saved, costs with no fixed date, and starting late. You'll also get a tracker you can copy into a spreadsheet or Notion, a comparison of places to keep the money, and a clear explanation of how sinking funds differ from an emergency fund. This is general education, not personal financial advice.

steps.name: List your non-monthly expenses
steps.text: Go through the last 12 months of bank and card statements. Note every cost you don't pay monthly: insurance premiums, registrations, renewals, memberships, trips, gifts, car servicing, home repairs and pet care.

steps.name: Set a target amount for each
steps.text: Use last year's bill, a renewal notice or a quote, not your memory. If the price went up at the last renewal, expect a similar rise and add it as a buffer.

steps.name: Find the due date and count contributions left
steps.text: Write down the next payment date. Then count how many transfers you'll make before it, whether those are monthly transfers or paydays. Costs with no fixed date get a rolling 12-month cycle.

steps.name: Subtract what you've already saved
steps.text: Take off any money already set aside for this expense, plus any deposit you've already paid. What's left is the real gap.

steps.name: Divide and round up
steps.text: Divide the gap by the number of contributions left, then round up to a whole dollar or the nearest $5. Example: ($1,200 − $300) ÷ 8 = $112.50, which rounds up to $115.

steps.name: Add up your funds and check affordability
steps.text: Add every fund's monthly amount to get one total transfer. If it doesn't fit your budget, fund essential bills first, then lower the targets or push back the dates for flexible goals like trips.

steps.name: Automate the transfers
steps.text: Set up a recurring transfer for the day after payday. Send it to one savings account split by a tracker, or to named sub-accounts if your bank offers them.

steps.name: Pay, reset and review
steps.text: Pay each bill from its fund, then switch that fund to its steady amount (annual cost ÷ 12). Every quarter, check your targets and due dates, and make sure the tracker's balances match your account.

sections.heading: What is a sinking fund?
paragraphs: A sinking fund is money you set aside in small, regular amounts so that a known future expense is already covered when the bill arrives.

For example, instead of paying a $1,200 insurance premium in one go, you save $100 a month for 12 months and pay with cash you already have. The term comes from corporate finance, where companies set money aside over time to repay debt. The household version is simpler: one pot of money for one predictable cost.

Most 'surprise' expenses aren't really surprises. Car insurance renews on the same date each year, the holidays arrive every December, and every roof needs work eventually. When no money is waiting for these costs, they tend to go on a credit card or slowly drain an emergency fund.
bullets: Good fits: costs where you can predict the amount, the timing or both, such as premiums, registrations, renewals, trips, gifts and upkeep.
Poor fits: bills you already pay monthly, which belong in your regular budget, and true emergencies like losing your job, which is what an emergency fund is for.
The goal: turn big once-a-year costs into one steady monthly number you can plan around.

sections.heading: How to calculate sinking funds for annual expenses: the formula
paragraphs: To calculate a sinking fund, subtract what you've already saved from the target amount, then divide by the number of contributions you'll make before the bill is due.

The formula is: Monthly contribution = (Target amount − Amount already saved) ÷ Contributions left before the due date. If you're starting from zero, it's just target ÷ months. A $600 bill due in 6 months needs $100 a month.

Count contributions, not calendar months. Say it's early October, the bill is due in mid-March, and you transfer money on the 1st of each month. You'll make five transfers (November 1 to March 1), so divide by 5, not 6. If you save from each paycheck, count the paydays left instead.

Base the target on real numbers: last year's bill, a renewal notice or a quote. If the price went up at the last renewal, expect a similar rise and build it in. Rounding the result up to a whole dollar, or the nearest $5, keeps transfers simple and gives you a small cushion.

Your first-year amount and your steady amount can be different. Once a fund is on track, the ongoing contribution for a yearly bill is just the annual cost ÷ 12. In the first year it can cost more per month if the bill is close. The catch-up section below explains how to handle that.
bullets: Target amount: the bill you expect, plus a buffer if prices tend to rise.
Already saved: money set aside for this specific expense, including any deposit you've already paid.
Contributions left: the transfers you'll actually make before the payment date.
Steady amount: annual cost ÷ 12, once the fund has caught up.

sections.heading: 6 sinking fund examples with worked numbers
paragraphs: Here are six common annual expenses worked through with the same formula. The comparison table sums them up. Every figure is a round placeholder, not a typical cost, so swap in your own bills. The method works the same in any currency.

Added together, these six funds need $855 a month in the first year and $755 a month once they're all at their steady amounts. That total is the number that matters for your budget, because it tells you before the bills arrive whether your plans are realistic.
If the total is more than you can spare, the system still works. Fund essential bills first, lower some targets, and give flexible goals like trips more time.
bullets: Car insurance: a $1,200 premium due in 12 months → $1,200 ÷ 12 = $100 a month. Some insurers charge more for monthly installments than for paying in full, so check your policy. Having the cash ready lets you choose whichever option costs less overall.

Holiday: a $3,000 trip in 10 months → $300 a month. If that doesn't fit, change one of the inputs. A $2,000 trip in 10 months, or the $3,000 trip pushed back to 15 months, both work out to $200 a month. If it's a yearly trip, the steady amount after this one is $250.

Car repairs and maintenance: these have no fixed date, so estimate a year's cost. Use the last two years of receipts plus anything you know is coming, such as new tires. If that comes to $900 → $75 a month, kept as a rolling balance.

Annual subscriptions: three renewals adding up to $360 that you've just paid → $360 ÷ 12 = $30 a month. If one renews sooner, give it its own countdown. A $120 renewal 3 months away needs $40 a month until it's paid.

Gifts: $600 for December plus $600 in birthdays spread across the year. Split them into two funds. Birthdays become a rolling $50 a month ($600 ÷ 12). December gets its own countdown: $600 ÷ 6 = $100 a month if you start in June. That's $150 a month for now, falling to $100 once December is on a 12-month cycle.

Home maintenance: list the jobs you know about, for example a $200 heating service and $200 for gutter cleaning, then add a repair buffer of, say, $2,000. That's a $2,400 target → $200 a month. A rough rule of thumb you'll often see is about 1% of a home's value per year, but real costs vary a lot with the home's age, condition and climate.

sections.heading: Handling money already saved and costs with no fixed date
paragraphs: If you've already saved part of the money, subtract it before dividing. If a cost has no fixed date, save your yearly estimate ÷ 12 each month and treat the fund as a rolling balance.
Partly saved example: your $1,200 car insurance is due in 8 months and you already have $300 set aside. ($1,200 − $300) ÷ 8 = $112.50 a month, which rounds up to $115.
Partly paid example: you've booked a $3,000 trip, paid a $500 deposit and saved another $1,000, with 5 months to go. $3,000 − $500 − $1,000 = $1,500, so $1,500 ÷ 5 = $300 a month.

Rolling funds are for costs like car repairs, home repairs, vet bills and replacing a phone. Divide your best yearly estimate by 12 and save that every month. When something breaks, pay from the fund and keep saving so it fills back up.
bullets: Set a cap, such as one year's estimate. When a rolling fund reaches it, pause the transfers and send that money to another goal.
Check rolling funds every quarter. If a fund keeps running dry, your estimate is too low. If it sits untouched for a year, the estimate may be too high.
Recalculate whenever a renewal notice shows a new price.
Don't count the same money twice: cash in one fund can't also count as 'already saved' in another.

sections.heading: How to catch up when you start late
paragraphs: If you start late, divide what's still missing by the contributions you have left, accept a higher payment for now, and drop back to the normal amount once the bill is paid.

Example: your $1,200 insurance renews in 4 months and you have nothing saved. $1,200 ÷ 4 = $300 a month for four months. After you pay the bill, the next renewal is 12 months away, so the payment drops to $100 a month. The higher amount is only temporary.
If the catch-up amount won't fit your budget, work through the options below roughly in order. The first ones don't involve debt.
Don't start a dozen funds in the same week. Begin with the bills due soonest and the ones where missing a payment hurts most. Add the rest as each catch-up period ends.
bullets: Add a lump sum: a tax refund, a bonus or money from selling things you no longer use can close the gap in one go.
Lower the target: shop around before renewals, cancel subscriptions you don't use, or choose a cheaper trip.
Move the date: flexible goals like holidays can often wait. Fixed bills like insurance usually can't.
Ask about installments: many providers let you pay monthly, but compare the total cost, because it can be higher than paying in full.
Put essentials first: a lapsed insurance policy or a late registration fee does more damage than a smaller holiday.
If you have to borrow, plan the payoff: a credit card can cover a short gap, but interest can quickly cancel out the benefit, so schedule the repayment.

sections.heading: Where to keep sinking funds: one account or sub-accounts?
paragraphs: Most people keep sinking funds in a savings account separate from everyday checking. That can be one account split by a tracker, or several named sub-accounts.

Bill money usually belongs in cash because you'll need it within months. Investments such as stocks can fall in value right before a bill is due. Crypto is an especially poor fit. Prices can swing sharply, you can lose everything to hacks, scams or an exchange failure, and crypto holdings generally don't get the deposit protection that regulated bank accounts have. Cash has a trade-off too: savings rates change over time and may not keep up with rising prices.

Before you open an account, check whether it's covered by your country's deposit protection scheme (such as FDIC insurance in the US or the FSCS in the UK) and what the limits are. Also check how fast transfers reach checking, whether there are monthly fees or minimum balances, and whether interest is taxable where you live. Terms change, so confirm the details on the provider's website.
bullets: One savings account plus a tracker: one account, one transfer, one interest rate. The bank only shows one total, so you need a spreadsheet or Notion page to know what belongs to each fund. Without one, a big balance can look like spare money.

Sub-accounts at one bank (often called buckets, pots, spaces or vaults): each fund gets its own balance in your banking app, so you can see right away when one is short. Not every bank offers them. Check how many you can open, whether each one earns interest and whether there are fees.
Separate accounts at different banks: strong separation for a few large funds, such as a major home project. The cost is more logins, more transfers and possibly minimum balances.
Leaving it in checking: no setup, but it's easy to spend by accident and usually earns little or no interest.

sections.heading: A simple sinking fund tracker (spreadsheet or Notion layout)
paragraphs: A sinking fund tracker needs one row per fund and a few columns that work out each month's contribution for you.

In Google Sheets or Excel, put each fund on its own row starting at row 2 and use the columns below. The formulas are written for row 2, so fill them down for the other rows. DATEDIF counts whole months, which usually matches monthly transfers. If your schedule is different, adjust the number by hand.

Add a second tab called Log with four columns: Date, Fund, Amount (positive for deposits, negative for withdrawals) and Note. Once a month, check that the Saved column adds up to your real account balance. If it doesn't, a transaction is missing from the log.

In Notion, create a database called Sinking Funds with three properties: Target (number), Due (date) and Saved. Saved can be a number you type in, or a rollup that adds up a linked Transactions database. Then add two formula properties. Months left: max(dateBetween(prop("Due"), now(), "months"), 1). Monthly: ceil(max(prop("Target") - prop("Saved"), 0) / prop("Months left")). Turn on Sum under the Monthly column to see your total. Notion's formula syntax can change, so check its formula help pages.
Add the monthly total to your main budget as one line, so it gets planned alongside rent, groceries and debt payments.
bullets: A – Fund: the name, e.g. Car insurance.
B – Target: the amount you expect to pay. For rolling funds, use your cap.
C – Due date: the next payment date.
D – Months left: =MAX(1, IFERROR(DATEDIF(TODAY(), C2, "M"), 1))
E – Saved: type in the balance, or total it from the Log tab with =SUMIF(Log!B:B, A2, Log!C:C)
F – Monthly needed: =ROUNDUP(MAX(0, B2-E2)/D2, 0). For rolling funds, type a fixed amount (annual estimate ÷ 12) instead.
G – Status: =IF(E2>=B2, "Funded", "Saving")
Total: =SUM(F2:F20) gives your total monthly sinking-fund transfer. Extend the range if you have more funds.

sections.heading: Sinking fund vs. emergency fund: what's the difference?
paragraphs: A sinking fund pays for expenses you can predict. An emergency fund covers the ones you can't, such as losing your job or an urgent repair you had no reason to expect.

Keeping them separate protects both. If holiday money and emergency money share one pot with no tracker, a planned trip can slowly eat into your safety net, and you won't notice until something actually goes wrong.

Some costs fall in between. Routine servicing and new tires belong in a sinking fund. A major breakdown that costs more than your car fund holds may have to come from the emergency fund. A simple test: if you can name the expense and roughly predict when it will happen, it's a sinking-fund cost.
bullets: Purpose: a sinking fund is for planned, known costs. An emergency fund is for unplanned, unknown ones.
Size: sinking funds are sized bill by bill. Emergency funds are usually sized as a number of months of essential expenses.
Spending: a sinking fund is meant to be spent, so hitting zero after paying the bill means it worked. An emergency fund should stay untouched for as long as possible.
After use: a sinking fund goes back to its steady monthly amount. An emergency fund should be refilled as a priority.

recommendations.best_for: People who want a customizable sinking fund tracker that works out months left and monthly contributions with formula and rollup properties, kept next to their other household notes and plans. Check Notion's website for current plans and limits.
recommendations.not_for: Anyone who wants balances pulled in from their bank automatically. Notion isn't a banking or budgeting app, so you enter or log balances yourself. It's also not worth switching if you already have a spreadsheet tracker that works.

faq.question: How much should I put in a sinking fund each month?
faq.answer: Subtract what you've already saved from the target amount, then divide by the number of contributions left before the bill is due. For a $1,200 bill due in 12 months with nothing saved, that's $100 a month. Once a fund has caught up, the ongoing amount for a yearly bill is the annual cost divided by 12.

faq.question: How do I calculate a sinking fund if I'm paid every two weeks?
faq.answer: Divide what you still need by the number of paydays left before the due date. A $1,200 bill due in about 12 months gives you roughly 26 paydays, so about $46.15 per paycheck, rounded up to $47. Saving a fixed amount from each paycheck also saves you from recalculating in months with three paydays.

faq.question: How many sinking funds should I have?
faq.answer: Have enough to cover every non-monthly expense that would strain your budget if it arrived without warning. Many people start with their three to five biggest or soonest bills and put small items, like minor subscriptions, into one shared fund. Add more only once the first ones are running smoothly.

faq.question: Should I keep sinking funds in a high-yield savings account?
faq.answer: Many people do, because the money stays easy to reach and earns some interest while it waits. Rates change over time, so check fees, withdrawal limits and transfer times, and whether the account is covered by your country's deposit protection scheme. Interest may also be taxable depending on where you live.

faq.question: Can I use my emergency fund for annual bills instead?
faq.answer: You can, but you'll have a smaller safety net if a real emergency happens at the same time. Annual bills are predictable, which is exactly why a separate sinking fund suits them better. If you do dip into your emergency fund, plan how and when you'll pay it back.

faq.question: What should I do with leftover money in a sinking fund?
faq.answer: If a bill comes in under your target, you can leave the extra in the fund and lower next year's monthly amount, or move it to another fund that's running short. Either way, update your tracker so the Saved column still matches your real account balance.

conclusion: Calculating sinking funds comes down to one formula: what you still need, divided by the contributions you have left. Apply it to every non-monthly bill you can name. Start with the bills due soonest, automate the transfers, and let a simple tracker do the math. After one full cycle, most funds settle at the annual cost ÷ 12, and once-a-year bills stop feeling like emergencies. For decisions about specific accounts, tax on interest or wider financial planning, check your local regulator's guidance or talk to a licensed adviser.
